tldr: When a humanoid robot receives an emergency stop command, the proposed task-agnostic framework "Safe-Stop" uses two complementary estimators to judge whether a safe stop is even feasible from the current state, immediately handing off to a fall mitigation policy if it is not. It achieved a 96.4% stopping success rate on unseen motion data, while driving the false positive rate—mistakenly classifying an unstoppable state as stoppable—down to just 3.89%.
hero_caption: Relationship between the difficulty score measured during motion tracking (the maximum reach-avoid value during a pre-scan) and the emergency stop failure rate. When the difficulty is 0.6 or below, stopping is virtually safe in both simulation and the real robot; however, the failure rate spikes above 0.85, demonstrating that the learned value function accurately ranks real-world stopping risk.
overview:
As humanoid robots increasingly operate in shared human environments, reliable safety during emergency stops is essential. However, conventional control typically handles a stop signal simply by setting the target velocity to zero and relying on the standard locomotion controller to decelerate. When the robot is running fast, twisting aggressively, or mid-air during a flight phase—exceeding physical recovery limits—attempting to force an upright stop can lead to violent collisions and damage.

To address this, the authors cast emergency stopping as a reach-avoid problem: reaching a safe stopped state while avoiding falls. The proposed method, Safe-Stop, learns two platform-specific components: a stop policy that handles "how to stop" and two complementary estimators that assess "whether stopping is truly feasible from the current state." The estimators consist of a stop-probability critic supervised by the empirical outcomes of the stop policy itself, and a reach-avoidance value function based on physical states via Hamilton-Jacobi reachability.

During online deployment, Safe-Stop continues the upright stop only if both estimators agree within a recent short time window that a safe stop remains feasible; if either indicates danger, it immediately switches to a fall policy instantiated as damping fallback. Because neither the stop policy nor the estimators depend on upstream task-specific information, once trained on walking data, they transfer directly to entirely different upstream tasks such as motion tracking or manipulation without retraining.

In large-scale simulation and physical validation using the Unitree G1 robot across approximately 180,000 trials initialized from unseen human motion data, Safe-Stop achieved a 96.4% stopping success rate. Furthermore, it suppressed the critical false positive rate—mistakenly treating an unstoppable failure state as stoppable—to just 3.89%, demonstrating that its risk estimation functions accurately on hardware as well.
contributions: Formulated a task-agnostic emergency stop framework decoupled into three layers: "how to stop (stop policy)," "whether stopping is feasible (stoppability estimation)," and "whether to commit to stopping or switch to fall mitigation (runtime agreement)."

Proposed two complementary estimators—a stop-probability critic learned from stop policy execution outcomes and a reach-avoidance value function learned over physical states—paired with an agreement window switching rule for high-precision decisions.
Discovered that masking arm joint information to focus solely on torso and leg support significantly improves stoppability estimation accuracy on unseen, out-of-distribution (OOD) motions.

Achieved a 96.4% stopping success rate across roughly 180,000 unseen motion evaluations with the Unitree G1, and demonstrated on physical hardware that the stopping difficulty score strongly correlates with actual fall risk.

sections.heading: Why "Just Stop" Can Sometimes Be Dangerous
sections.summary: When given an emergency stop command, merely decelerating can worsen falls from marginal states. What robots need at runtime is the ability to judge whether to attempt an upright stop or immediately transition to fall mitigation. This paper proposes "Safe-Stop," a novel emergency stopping mechanism that transfers across upstream tasks from a single training run.
sections.details:
As humanoids are deployed in collaborative human environments, reliable, low-risk emergency stopping is becoming critical. However, when an emergency stop is triggered, most existing systems simply set the target velocity to zero, relying on the normal locomotion controller's restorative capabilities to decelerate.

This approach only works within the robot's stable basin of attraction. When running at high speeds, twisting the body severely, or in a flight phase where feet are off the ground, physical recovery limits are already breached; attempting to force an upright stop is far more dangerous. Rather than tumbling uncontrollably, switching proactively to fall mitigation reduces damage to both the robot and its surroundings.

Prior studies have explored fall prediction and fall-arrest controllers, but most are trained conditioned on the behaviors of a specific walking policy. Consequently, whenever the task changes from walking to manipulation or whole-body tracking, failure data must be recollected and models retrained from scratch. A baseline safety system should be built once per robot hardware platform and work across all tasks.

To achieve this, the authors propose Safe-Stop, comprising an upstream-independent stop policy and two stoppability estimators. In experiments with the Unitree G1 in the NVIDIA Isaac Lab simulator across 179,650 test trials from unseen motion data, Safe-Stop achieved a 96.4% stopping success rate and suppressed dangerous false positives to just 3.89%.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Locomotion, Fall Prediction, and Reach-Avoidance
sections.summary: This work combines insights from reinforcement learning for bipedal locomotion, impact mitigation during falls, fall prediction, and reach-avoid theory. While prior work focused on post-fall protection or policy-dependent prediction, Safe-Stop stands out by evaluating whether a dedicated stop policy can successfully halt the robot right after the command, completely independent of the upstream task.
sections.details:
To clarify where this research sits, let us examine its relationship to four related fields:

### RL-Based Bipedal Locomotion Control
Deep reinforcement learning (such as PPO) combined with domain randomization has enabled agile walking, blind rough-terrain traversal, and whole-body motion tracking. However, these focus primarily on command tracking and disturbance rejection; they do not incorporate the ability to autonomously decide whether a safe stop is currently feasible.

### Fall Mitigation and Fall Prediction
When stopping is impossible, the next priority is mitigating contact impact during a fall. Approaches using model predictive control or RL to break falls (such as SafeFall) have been proposed. Fall predictors using IMUs or neural networks also detect impending falls. However, these learn when a *specific nominal walking policy* breaks down, meaning changing the policy requires retraining the predictor. Safe-Stop assesses feasibility based on the stop policy's outcomes and underlying physical states, keeping it task-agnostic.

### Safe RL and Reach-Avoid Analysis
Unlike safe RL, which focuses on avoiding unsafe regions during training, Safe-Stop addresses switching safety at deployment time. Drawing inspiration from Hamilton-Jacobi reach-avoid analysis in control theory, it approximates a value function over the high-dimensional humanoid state space to assess whether the robot can reach a target set (quiescence) while avoiding a failure set (falling).

sections.heading: Casting Emergency Stop as a Reach-Avoid Problem
sections.summary: By defining upright quiescence as the target set and falling as the failure set, the set of states from which the robot can reach the target before failing under a fixed stop policy is defined as the "stoppable set." This allows stoppability to be evaluated purely through the current physical state and the stop policy, regardless of what the upstream task was.
sections.details:
Prior to an emergency stop, the robot operates under an arbitrary upstream behavior policy $\pi_{\mathrm{bhvr}}$, such as walking, tracking, or manipulation. At the moment the stop command arrives, $t_{\mathrm{stop}}$, the system detaches from the upstream policy and selects between executing a learned stop policy $\pi_{\mathrm{stop}}$ or a fall policy $\pi_{\mathrm{fall}}$ (instantiated as simple damping control in this paper).

Here, an upright, nearly quiescent state with stable foot contact is designated as the target set $\mathcal{G}_{\text{stop}}$, and falling or breaking limits constitutes the failure set $\mathcal{F}$. Under a fixed stop policy $\pi_{\mathrm{stop}}$, the collection of initial states that reach the target set before falling into the failure set is defined as the "stoppable set" $\mathcal{E}_{\text{stop}}$.

This distinction is crucial: whether a given state $s_t$ belongs to $\mathcal{E}_{\text{stop}}$ depends entirely on the properties of state $s_t$ and the stop policy $\pi_{\mathrm{stop}}$, completely independent of which upstream task policy $\pi_{\mathrm{bhvr}}$ was being executed beforehand. This decouples the stopping decision into a standalone, task-agnostic safety foundation.

sections.heading: A Dual-Estimator Architecture Decoupling Control from Feasibility
sections.summary: Safe-Stop learns a whole-body braking stop policy alongside two complementary stoppability estimators: a stop-probability critic and a reach-avoid value function. At runtime, the stop policy is permitted only if all estimators agree across a recent time window; if agreement breaks, execution immediately hands off to fall mitigation.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Learning the Stop Policy ($\pi_{\text{stop}}$)
The stop policy is trained to engage after an emergency stop command triggered from randomized locomotion states. Its input observation vector $o_t^{\mathrm{stop}}$ contains only proprioceptive information—gravity vector, base angular velocity, joint position errors/velocities, and the previous action—omitting upstream task targets, reference trajectories, and global positions entirely. The reward design employs velocity-gated regularization: at high speeds, it avoids forcing an immediate upright posture, prioritizing forceful braking foot placement first and encouraging an upright quiescent posture only after the robot decelerates.

### 4.2 Dual Stoppability Estimation
Even if a policy learns how to stop, whether it can actually succeed from a given state is another question. Thus, two complementary estimator networks are trained concurrently:

- **Stop-Probability Critic ($\hat{P}_{\phi}$)**: Predicts the empirical probability that executing the stop policy will reach the target set without falling. Using TD learning with a discount factor extremely close to 1 ($0.999999$), it outputs the final stopping success probability in $[0, 1]$.
- **Reach-Avoid (RA) Value Function ($\hat{V}_{\psi}$)**: Estimates physical state-based danger via a Bellman backup inspired by Hamilton-Jacobi theory. Defining an avoidance margin $g(s)$ capturing base height drop and trunk tilt, and an activation signal $l(s)$ indicating remaining base velocity, it uses Bellman equations combining $\max$ and $\min$ to evaluate reachability to quiescence while avoiding failure.

Two estimators are necessary because the probability critic captures the learned controller's emergent behavior, while the RA value function captures conservative physical boundary limits. Requiring agreement between both prevents the single failure mode of one estimator from being overlooked, thoroughly suppressing the most dangerous error: false positives (mistakenly classifying an unstoppable state as stoppable).

### 4.3 Runtime Decision Layer and Agreement Window
Because instantaneous estimates near decision boundaries can be noisy, Safe-Stop evaluates a backward time window of the most recent $K$ samples. It continues the stop policy only when $\hat{P}_{\phi} \geq \eta_p$ and $\hat{V}_{\psi} \leq \eta_r$ hold across all $K$ steps; if even a single step violates the thresholds, it immediately hands off to the fall policy via damping. Looking back over past samples introduces zero decision latency.

sections.heading: Validation on 180k Unseen Motion Episodes and Physical Unitree G1
sections.summary: When Safe-Stop, trained purely on locomotion, was evaluated on 179,650 unseen human motion episodes (BONES-SEED), it achieved a 96.4% stopping success rate and an AUC exceeding 0.97. The estimated difficulty score strongly correlated with real-world failure rates on the physical Unitree G1, and ablations confirmed the effectiveness of the dual estimators and the backward agreement window.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used the Unitree G1 humanoid (29 DOFs) across 4,096 parallel environments in Isaac Lab at a control frequency of 50 Hz. Pre-stop states were generated using an omnidirectional locomotion policy, with stop commands issued randomly between 0.2 and 1.0 seconds after episode onset.

### 5.2 Zero-Shot Transfer from Unseen States
The frozen stop policy and estimators, trained only on locomotion data, were applied to unseen states initialized from arbitrary frames across over 140,000 human motions in the BONES-SEED dataset (179,650 episodes). Without retraining, Safe-Stop achieved a 96.4% stopping success rate. The estimators demonstrated remarkable discriminative accuracy, achieving ROC AUCs of 0.971 for the probability critic, 0.969 for the RA value function, and 0.972 for the combined score.

### 5.3 Real-Time RA-Triggered Experiments and Hardware Validation
Using 59 motion tracking clips, the authors defined the pre-scanned peak RA value as the "clip difficulty score $d$." Stopping attempts triggered at these high-risk moments resulted in only 9 failures out of 510 trials for difficulty $d \leq 0.6$, whereas all 30/30 trials failed for $d > 1.0$, yielding a Spearman rank correlation of $\rho = 0.689$.
Furthermore, running 5 distinct motion clips (H1–H5, 30 trials each, 150 trials total) on the physical Unitree G1 revealed a sharp failure rate increase on high-difficulty clips, mirroring simulation and confirming that the learned value function acts as a faithful real-world risk metric.

### 5.4 Ablation Analysis
Ablating the agreement window and dual estimation revealed that requiring agreement over the past $K=5$ steps slashed the false positive rate (FPR) by 73% compared to instantaneous checks ($K=1$), reaching 3.89%. Additionally, masking arm joint inputs from the estimators improved the failure catch rate on unseen motions by approximately 4%. Removing task-specific arm posture noise directly leads to more robust stopping decisions.

captions.F4: Evolution of estimator values over steps following an emergency stop command. In true positive trials (TP: green), both estimators remain stably within safe margins. In false positive trials attempting to stop but failing (FP: red), the probability $\hat{P}_\phi$ drops sharply and danger $\hat{V}_\psi$ surges as steps progress. This visually highlights how tracking the trajectory over a multi-step window effectively filters out misjudgments.

sections.heading: Looking Forward: Advanced Fall Policies and "Wait-Then-Stop" Decisions
sections.summary: While Safe-Stop dramatically reduces emergency stop risks, its current fallback remains simple damping control. Furthermore, reasoning about transient dynamic states—such as continuing the current motion briefly before halting—remains an open challenge.
sections.details:
Although Safe-Stop substantially elevates emergency stopping safety, it has clear limitations.

First, when a state is deemed unstoppable, the fallback fall policy is currently implemented as simple whole-body damping. To minimize hardware damage further, integrating advanced fall-arrest controllers that optimize contact sequences or roll maneuvers, as seen in prior work, will be essential.

Second, the framework does not reason about transient temporal opportunities—such as scenarios where stopping right away causes a fall, but continuing the upstream motion for another 0.2 seconds until foot touchdown would allow a perfectly safe stop. Currently, Safe-Stop only evaluates stoppability at the exact instant the command arrives; expanding it to reason about short-term delays until a safe stopping window opens is a promising future direction.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Task-Agnostic Safety Infrastructure for Humanoids
sections.summary: Safe-Stop secures humanoid emergency stops by pairing a learned stop policy with task-agnostic stoppability estimators and window-agreement runtime switching. Exhibiting strong generalization to unseen motions, it serves as a practical, reusable safety foundation for hardware platforms.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Safe-Stop, a framework that decouples humanoid emergency stopping into three independent roles: stop execution, stoppability estimation, and runtime safety switching.

In extensive simulation on the Unitree G1, models trained solely on locomotion tasks achieved an exceptional 96.4% stopping success rate on unseen human motions. Moreover, by combining a stop-probability critic and a physics-based reach-avoid value function in an agreement window, the framework drove the dangerous false positive rate down to 3.89% (precision 99.78%).

Physical robot experiments verified that the learned risk scores accurately predict actual fall risks. Requiring no retraining across upstream tasks and trained once per robot platform, Safe-Stop offers an indispensable safety foundation for humanoids deployed in the real world.

sections.heading: Appendix: Reward Design, Arm Masking, and Damage Evaluation
sections.summary: The appendix details velocity-dependent reward formulation, reach-avoid signal definitions, the positive impact of arm masking on value function geometry, contact-force-based broken score damage evaluations, and comparisons against SafeFall-style baselines.
sections.details:
### Stop Policy Reward Design and Reach-Avoid Signals
In stop policy training, upright posture rewards are modulated by a velocity-dependent weight $\sigma(v) = \exp(-v^2/v_0^2)$. This prioritizes forceful foot braking at high speeds and defers upright alignment until velocity drops. In reach-avoid signals, the avoidance term $g(s)$ is clipped based on base height ($< 0.36$ m) and trunk tilt ($> 0.8$ rad), while the activation term $l(s)$ remains positive until base velocity drops below $0.1$ m/s.

### Value Function Stabilization via Arm Masking
A detailed ablation investigates masking 14 arm joints (positions, velocities, previous actions, totaling 42 dimensions) from estimator inputs. Retaining arm states confuses estimators with task-specific arm motions; restricting inputs to leg and torso support signals substantially improves failure detection on unseen data. Value function landscapes show that the arm-masked model produces the smoothest, most physically consistent decision boundaries.

### Damage Evaluation via Broken Score and Baseline Comparisons
Evaluating contact forces scaled by body part vulnerability weights (head/torso: 10, ankles/shoulders: 1, knees/elbows: 0.1) into a "broken score" revealed that Safe-Stop's dual-estimator rule diverted 96.2% of impending failure trials into the fall policy, cutting worst-5% collision impacts from 817 down to 440. Compared to conventional GRU predictors like SafeFall that detect falls only after instability begins, Safe-Stop assesses stoppability up front, achieving vastly higher selectivity and reduced impact damage.

captions.F5: Stopping success rate by initial base velocity across unseen motion data. Success rates stay above 94% below 2 m/s, but plummet sharply between 2 and 3 m/s, confirming physical recovery limits and the necessity of state-dependent stoppability estimation rather than a single fixed velocity threshold.
captions.F6: Calibration diagrams for the stop-probability critic (left) and reach-avoid (RA) safety score (right) on unseen motion data. Predicted values align closely with actual empirical success rates along the diagonal, showing that both estimators accurately capture probabilities and risk on out-of-distribution motions.
captions.F7: ROC curves for stoppability classification on unseen motion data. The probability critic alone achieves an AUC of 0.971, the RA value function alone achieves 0.969, and their combined decision reaches an AUC of 0.972, demonstrating outstanding discriminative performance.
captions.F8: Scatter plot comparisons of decision regions by estimator: RA value alone (left), stop probability alone (center), and their combined agreement (right). Applying the agreement rule (right) eliminates regions mistakenly classified as stoppable (red FP points), visually illustrating the drop in false positive rate to 18.5%.
captions.F10: Reach-avoid (RA) value function landscape comparisons across different input masks. The center "arm-masked (retaining legs + pelvis)" maintains smooth, physically consistent boundaries (black line: V=0) across upright, forward-lean, and backward-lean poses. In contrast, full observations (top) distort boundaries with irrelevant arm shifts, and masking legs (bottom) flattens the landscape due to lost support information.

takeaways: Decoupling "how to stop" (control) from "can it stop at all" (feasibility estimation) prevents over-forcing the controller and enables safe handoff to fall mitigation.
Enforcing agreement between an empirical success probability critic (TD learning) and a physical reach-avoid boundary function dramatically cuts fatal false positives.
Masking task-dependent arm joints and focusing on torso and leg support state is essential for out-of-distribution task generalization in stoppability estimation.
Conditioning the framework entirely on platform proprioception rather than upstream tasks makes it a universal, reusable safety layer learned once per robot hardware platform.
limitations: The fall policy is currently simple joint damping (approximating limp collapse), lacking active contact sequencing or roll maneuvers to deliberately minimize fall impact.
The framework only evaluates the instant the command arrives, ignoring potential short delays—such as taking one more step to plant both feet—that could enable a safe stop.
Hardware evaluations exhibit baseline noise (roughly 3–10% baseline failure) due to real-world contact discrepancies, state estimation error, and communication latency.
